newsitem.title: USA: NYC faces $2.5 bln gap in FY 1998 - NY state monitor.
newsitem.headline: NYC faces $2.5 bln gap in FY 1998 - NY state monitor.

text.p: The New York State Financial Control Board, an important fiscal monitor for New York City, on Tuesday estimated the city's 1998 fiscal budget contained risks that totaled approximately $2.473 billion.

The Board, in a report on the city's finances that was released the same day, projected the risk in the city's 1997 fiscal budget at $286 million, but noted that, if the state legislature extends a personal income tax surcharge, this estimate would fall by $171 million.

Similarly, if the state legislature approves an extension of the New York City personal income tax surcharge for fiscal year 1998, this would cut the risk by the $463 million of revenues that the levy is projected to produce.
New York State Gov. George Pataki said Tuesday there was an "excellent chance" of approving the personal income tax surcharge at the special session he called to start Tuesday.

The Giuliani Administration, in its November budget modification, said there would no gap in fiscal year 1997, partly due to a surprising $450 million jump in tax revenues, while it sees a $1.226 billion gap in fiscal year 1998. Alan Hevesi, the city comptroller, has said the strong performance by Wall Street financial houses could help the city end the current fiscal year with a more than $300 million surplus.
The state board also said that a proposed new infrastructure authority, which Pataki also said the legislature likely would approve, might have to issue $6 billion of debt through fiscal year 2000.

There is no assurance the city ultimately will win in a court fight over whether it can sell the water and sewer system, and if it fails to do so, it would need find another $1 billion to replace this source of pay-as-you-go financing, bringing the total to $6 bilion.
